title: What is the role of leader and follower replicas, and what is the in-sync replica set (ISR)?
shortTitle: Leader and follower replicas and the in-sync replica set (ISR)
keyPoints: Each partition has one leader replica that handles all reads and writes, and one or more follower replicas that passively copy data from the leader.
The ISR (In-Sync Replica set) is the leader plus all followers caught up within `replica.lag.time.max.ms`, and only ISR members can be elected leader.
With `acks=all`, the leader acknowledges a write only after every ISR member has copied it, providing the strongest durability guarantee.
`min.insync.replicas` sets the floor: if the ISR shrinks below this number, the leader rejects writes rather than risk data loss.
Unclean leader election (`unclean.leader.election.enable=true`) promotes an out-of-sync replica and risks data loss; it is disabled in banking systems.
Monitoring ISR-shrink events is critical because a chronically shrinking ISR signals an unhealthy broker that threatens durability.

s1_definition.oneliner: The leader serves all reads and writes, followers copy it, and the ISR is the caught-up replicas eligible to take over.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Leader replica** – the single replica of a partition that handles all producer writes and consumer reads, maintaining the authoritative ordered log.
- **Follower replica** – a passive copy of the partition that continuously fetches records from the leader to stay current, ready to be promoted if the leader fails.
- **In-Sync Replica set (ISR)** – the dynamic subset of replicas (leader plus caught-up followers) that have replicated all committed records within the lag window defined by `replica.lag.time.max.ms`.
- **`acks=all`** – the producer acknowledgment setting where the leader confirms a write only after every replica in the current ISR has stored it.
- **`min.insync.replicas`** – a topic or broker setting that defines the minimum number of replicas that must acknowledge a write under `acks=all`; if the ISR shrinks below this, writes are rejected.
- **Unclean leader election** – promoting a replica that is not in the ISR, which risks losing committed records; disabled by default in modern Kafka.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps a transaction ledger in three identical copies in three different branches for safety. One branch is the official branch (the leader) where all new entries are written and all queries are answered. The other two branches (followers) constantly copy every new entry so they match. The set of branches that are fully up to date is the in-sync set. If the official branch burns down, the bank promotes one of the fully up-to-date copies to become the new official branch, and no entries are lost.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Leader, Followers, and ISR
===========================

  Partition: transfers-P2 (RF=3)

  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Broker 1 (LEADER)    │
  │ Offset: 0..100       │◀── Producer writes here
  │ Serves reads/writes  │──▶ Consumer reads here
  └──────────┬───────────┘
             │ Followers fetch
    ┌────────┴────────┐
    │                 │
    ▼                 ▼
  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
  │ Broker 2 (F) │  │ Broker 3 (F) │
  │ Offset: 0..100│  │ Offset: 0..98 │
  │ IN SYNC      │  │ LAGGING      │
  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘

  ISR = {Broker1, Broker2}  (Broker3 fell out)

  acks=all write:
  Producer -> Broker1 stores -> Broker2 stores -> ACK
  (Broker3 not in ISR, not waited for)

  Leader failure:
  Broker1 crashes -> Controller elects Broker2 (ISR member)
  ISR = {Broker2(new LEADER)}
  No committed data lost.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
In Kafka, every partition is replicated across several brokers, with one elected as the leader and the rest as followers. The leader handles all reads and writes, keeping ordering simple because there is a single authoritative log. Followers continuously fetch records from the leader to stay caught up, and their only job is to be ready to take over if the leader fails.

The ISR is the heart of Kafka's durability model. It is the leader plus every follower that is caught up within the lag window. With `acks=all`, the leader only acknowledges a write after every ISR member has stored it, and `min.insync.replicas` sets the floor so the leader refuses writes if the ISR shrinks too small. When the leader's broker dies, the controller elects a new leader from the ISR, ensuring no committed data is lost.

At National Bank of India, transfer topics run with replication factor three, `acks=all`, and `min.insync.replicas=2`. A committed transfer always lives on at least two brokers, the system tolerates one broker failure, and if the leader crashes a caught-up replica takes over with no lost transfers. Unclean leader election is disabled because promoting an out-of-sync replica could lose committed transfers.

Remember one sentence: the ISR is the set of caught-up replicas that acknowledges writes under `acks=all` and provides the candidates for leader election, making it the foundation of Kafka's durability.
